title: UNH Manchester Students Earn Top Research Awards - University of New Hampshire
content: Two University of New Hampshire at Manchester students earned top honors for their undergraduate research at the 2026 New Hampshire IDeA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence (NH-INBRE) Annual Meeting, held in August at the Omni Mount Washington Resort in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. The annual meeting brought together 290 students, faculty, administrators, and participants from other New Hampshire research programs to share discoveries, build connections, and celebrate advances in biomedical science. UNH Manchester was well represented, with two students earning poster presentation awards and the university’s STEM-MoBILE offering hands-on biotechnology experiences for attendees. Caroline Heafield '26, a biotechnology graduate and Millyard Scholar, earned first place for her research poster, "Investigating the Aggregation Behavior of Malassezia Fungi within the Human Skin Microbiota." Caroline's research examines the behavior of Malassezia, a group of fungi naturally found on human skin, and how they aggregate within the skin's microbial community. Her work contributes to a better understanding of the complex interactions between microorganisms and their human hosts. The recognition builds on Heafield's growing research experience. Her interest in microbiology began in an antibiotic discovery course at UNH Manchester, where she investigated bacteria collected from soil samples. She later studied fungal pathogens in a summer research program at Dartmouth, and she received an Undergraduate Research Award from UNH's Hamel Center for Undergraduate Research to pursue an independent project exploring fungi as potential sources of new antibiotics. "The fact that I can have this experience as an undergraduate is incredible," Heafield says. Her experiences have helped shape her interest in pursuing graduate studies focused on microbiology and human-microbe interactions. Read more about Caroline's undergraduate research journey. Biotechnology major August Paquin ’29 presented the poster "Quantifying Ocular Pain in Mice Using Deep-Learning-Based Feature-Tracking Software," which earned second place. August’s research explores how deep-learning technology can be used to measure ocular pain in mice by tracking physical features. The work demonstrates the potential for computational tools to support biomedical research and improve methods for studying pain. UNH Manchester's presence at the meeting extended beyond student research presentations. The STEM Mobile Biofabrication Integrated Lab Experience (STEM-MoBILE) also participated in the event, giving attendees opportunities to explore biotechnology through interactive, hands-on experiences. The STEM-MoBILE is a traveling laboratory designed to introduce students and community members to biofabrication, an emerging field focused on producing human tissues using biological and synthetic materials. Through demonstrations, experiments, and opportunities to use laboratory equipment, the STEM-MoBILE makes complex scientific concepts accessible while introducing participants to educational and career opportunities in biotechnology and related fields. title: From Student Filmmaker to Regional Emmy Award Nominee - University of New Hampshire
content: Less than a year after graduating from the University of New Hampshire at Manchester, communication arts alumnus Logan Plante ’25 found himself at an awards ceremony celebrating some of the best television work in New England. A photojournalist at WMUR-TV, Logan was part of the station’s team nominated for a 2026 Boston/New England Regional Emmy Award in the Breaking/Spot News – Single Report category for their coverage of the Brown University shooter manhunt in New Hampshire. The team didn’t take home the award, but the nomination marked an exciting early milestone in Logan’s career. “Although we didn’t bring home the award, it was an honor to be recognized alongside some of the most talented people in the industry,” Plante said. Logan joined WMUR in August 2025, just months after earning his bachelor’s degree in communication arts from UNH Manchester. As a photojournalist, his work puts him behind the camera as news unfolds. Arriving on scene, gathering video, and talking with people, Logan turns what is happening in real time into a story viewers can understand. The Emmy-nominated Brown University story was a prime example. Logan recalled that the WMUR team was covering developments from three locations as the story unfolded. For him, doing that work well comes down to more than knowing how to operate a camera or edit video. “The ability to talk to people is essential,” he says. “You also need to be comfortable under pressure and be able to manage your time with tight deadlines.” His advice to aspiring journalists is to build confidence in the fundamentals: hone your communication skills, practice writing, learn editing software, and keep working at your craft. “Just actively trying to be the best at it, that’s what makes you better,” he says. Before he was covering breaking news, Logan was developing his storytelling skills as a communication arts student at UNH Manchester. Logan learned how to tell a compelling story from start to finish, building skills in media writing, video production, digital editing, and documentary filmmaking — skills he now relies on as a photojournalist. During his senior year, Logan put those skills to work on an award-winning project. His documentary about New Hampshire’s booming oyster farming industry earned first place in the Cinema Arts category at UNH Manchester’s Undergraduate Research Conference. The project brought together many of the abilities that shape his work in television news: finding an interesting angle, talking with people, capturing strong visuals, and editing those pieces into a meaningful story. Logan’s path from student documentarian to Regional Emmy Award nominee shows what’s possible with passion and grit. At WMUR, the stories are different every day, the deadlines are tighter, and the stakes are higher. But the core challenge is familiar: connect with people and find the best way to tell their stories. It’s exactly the kind of work Logan hoped to do. “I am passionate about storytelling and have an affinity for interesting people and places,” Logan says. “I want to tell stories that inform, engage, and resonate.” For students who picture themselves behind a camera, in an editing suite, or digging for a story no one else has told yet, Logan’s experience offers some simple advice: learn the tools, practice the craft, and get comfortable talking to people… then be ready when the story happens. Chenango Valley's Tiffani Schaefer commits to UNH women's soccer On Friday, Chenango Valley senior Tiffani Schaefer officially signed committed to play Division I soccer at the University of New Hampshire next Fall. Schaefer has been a member of the varsity team since she was in eighth grade, she is a two-time All-Conference selection, and a four-time Section IV champion. Schaefer finishes her high school soccer career with 52 goals and 30 assists. The signing does come with a twist though, Schaefer played midfield for the Warriors but is a goalkeeper for her travel soccer team at the Syracuse Development Academy. Schaefer says her signing will be for her to continue to be in between the pipes for the Wildcats. Overall, the Chenango Valley senior is a three-sport athlete and has won numerous Section IV titles for both soccer and girls lacrosse. Schaefer spoke on her time at Chenango Valley and what it means to her. "There's so many different people that I've met and so many memories and friendships that I've made that I'm hoping will last forever," said Schaefer. "Hopefully one day when I am playing Binghamton University, I will be able to see them all and that will hopefully come out and support me." Schaefer says she plans to major in exercise science as she pursues a career as an athletic trainer. title: Can UNH's Optum Rx Sustain Profit Growth as Prescription Volumes Fall? - TradingView
content: UnitedHealth Group Incorporated’s UNH Optum Rx delivered higher operating earnings despite declining prescription volumes in the third quarter of 2026. Stronger profitability, supported by biosimilar adoption and operational efficiencies, highlights the segment's resilience amid membership-related pressures. However, sustaining this momentum without a recovery in prescription activity remains a key challenge. Optum Rx revenues edged up to $39.9 billion from $39.7 billion a year earlier. Operating earnings increased 10.9% to $1.72 billion, expanding the operating margin to 4.3% from 3.9%. Adjusted prescriptions declined 5.1% to 393 million, reflecting membership losses at UnitedHealthcare and other customers. The contrasting trends suggest that improving operating performance is helping offset weaker prescription activity. Specialty pharmacy offers an additional growth opportunity. Management reported a 2.6% increase in specialty volumes during the quarter, supported by strong demand for complex therapies and expanding provider relationships. Optum Rx is also strengthening its integrated pharmacy services, including infusion offerings, while advancing transparent pharmacy benefit pricing. These initiatives could support customer retention, improve business mix and provide additional earnings opportunities. Nevertheless, continued membership attrition could restrict overall prescription growth, while evolving pharmacy pricing arrangements may influence future profitability. Sustained margin expansion will require disciplined cost management and successful execution of higher-value pharmacy services. Although the segment has demonstrated its ability to improve profitability amid softer volumes, a recovery in prescription activity would provide a more durable foundation for earnings growth through 2027. UnitedHealth's Medical sector peers, The Cigna Group CI and CVS Health Corporation CVS, also illustrate how business mix and operating discipline affect profitability. Cigna's Evernorth reported 6% growth in adjusted revenues in the third quarter of 2026, but adjusted pretax operating earnings declined 4%. Cigna’s Pharmacy Benefit Services earnings fell 22%, while Specialty and Care Services earnings rose 15%, partly reflecting biosimilar and specialty generic adoption. CVS's Health Services segment reported 9.5% revenue growth and a 2.7% increase in adjusted operating income during the quarter. Pharmacy claims processed increased 1.3% on a 30-day equivalent basis. Unlike Optum Rx, CVS reported volume growth, underscoring different operating dynamics across the industry. Shares of UnitedHealth have risen 22.8% year to date compared with the industry’s 25.7% growth. From a valuation standpoint, UNH trades at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 17.6 compared with the industry average of 15.68. UNH carries a Value Score of A. title: 100 Years of Hospitality: How UNH Is Preparing Students for What's Next - University of New Hampshire
content: Claire Boulanger ’27 (center), student general manager of the Gourmet Dinner, meets with fellow hospitality management students during preparations for the event at Wentworth by the Sea. The annual dinner celebrated 100 years of hospitality education at UNH. For Claire Boulanger ’27, the most important part of hospitality isn't the food, the atmosphere, or even flawless event execution. It's how people feel when they leave. As student general manager of the Gourmet Dinner, a signature hands-on learning experience for UNH hospitality management students, Boulanger helped lead this year's centennial celebration at Wentworth by the Sea in New Castle. “The experience represents everything I love about hospitality: bringing people together, making them feel welcome, and creating something they'll remember,” Boulanger says. That emphasis on human connection has helped define hospitality education at UNH for 100 years, even as the industry, career opportunities, and the program itself have evolved. Michaela Mazzei ’27 welcomes a guest during check-in for the Gourmet Dinner at Wentworth by the Sea. Founded in 1926, UNH’s hospitality management program was the first in New England and is the second-oldest in the country, after Cornell University. It began as a hotel administration program in the College of Life Sciences and Agriculture before becoming part of the Whittemore School of Business and Economics — now the Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics. In 2024, the program transitioned from a standalone bachelor's degree to an option within Paul's business administration program, giving students greater flexibility to combine hospitality management with other business disciplines. John Murtha ’75, chair of the UNH Hospitality Management Advisory Board and task force general manager for Omni Hotels & Resorts, says that business foundation has been central to the program's longevity. “It's very important today that students understand basic business and economic principles, including finance, marketing, macro and microeconomics, and analytics," Murtha says. Garrison Dominguez ’18, assistant general manager at York Harbor Inn in Maine, experienced that versatility firsthand. Early in his career, an unexpected opportunity led him into hotel accounting, a role outside his preferred area of operations. “I'm more of a people person than a spreadsheet guy,” Dominguez says. “But the program gave us the background to step into roles that might not be our strengths and still be successful.” Hospitality management alums have built careers across the country, from New England's historic hotels and resorts to major hospitality companies such as Marriott International, Hilton, and Four Seasons. Murtha hired roughly two dozen UNH graduates while leading the Omni Parker House. “They come out with a strong work ethic. They're humble, they listen, and they want to succeed," Murtha says. "They're also willing to pay their dues." The program's two advisory boards — the Hospitality Management Advisory Board and the Board of Young Hospitality Professionals — bring together established industry leaders and recent graduates to advise on curriculum, mentor students, and connect them with internships and career opportunities. Those connections helped Dominguez as a student and inspired him to give back as a board member. “We had opportunities to get in front of decision-makers at major companies like Hilton, Marriott, Four Seasons, and Kimpton Hotels, which is where I went to work after graduation," Dominguez says. "Having that face time was invaluable. It gave us an idea of how to act, what to say, and how to speak with industry professionals while we were still juniors and seniors in college.” For today's students, the program's emphasis on industry connections and hands-on learning helps them build leadership skills long before graduation. Leading a large team of her peers for the Gourmet Dinner tested Boulanger’s leadership skills. "Experiences like Gourmet Dinner, event planning, leadership in my sorority, and a summer internship as an operations manager have helped me grow in confidence and find my strengths as a leader," Boulanger says. "I’ve learned how much I enjoy bringing people together around a shared goal and helping a team succeed." Katie Danaher ’28, who served as public relations officer and creative director for the Gourmet Dinner, enjoys the range of hospitality management. Along with gaining experience at a five-star resort, she works at the UNH Entrepreneurship Center and is president of Eta Sigma Delta, the hospitality honor society, where she built a website that connects students with alums. "Making people happy and providing services that make people feel cared about is what fulfills me," Danaher says. "UNH has given me countless opportunities to get involved in everything I could think of to learn and grow.” Krista Marvel (right), lecturer and hospitality management option coordinator, works with a student during Gourmet Dinner preparations in the kitchen at Wentworth by the Sea. As the hospitality industry evolves, Krista Marvel, lecturer and hospitality management option coordinator, sees an increasing emphasis on creating meaningful customer experiences. “We're really focused on customer service management and how you create experiences for guests or customers,” Marvel says. “There's a concept called narrative hospitality. Rather than simply providing a product or service, you're guiding guests through an entire experience, bringing together all the elements of a business to create something memorable.” That focus is opening doors beyond traditional hospitality settings. Marvel points to students working at companies like Fidelity, where they plan internal employee events and gatherings for other stakeholders. Hands-on learning through industry visits, job shadowing, and event planning remains central to preparing students for those opportunities. “The hospitality industry of tomorrow is going to be much broader than it has been,” Marvel says. “I tell my students all the time that hospitality can take you anywhere. Your career can look very different depending on which sector you pursue, and that gives you enormous flexibility throughout your career.” Danaher is bullish on the industry’s future and sees artificial intelligence (AI) renewing people’s appreciation for the personal touch. "I am starting to see people become exhausted from AI integration in other parts of their lives and see them feeling refreshed when good human customer service is provided," Danaher says. Lucy Gilson, dean of Paul College, believes the program's greatest strengths will remain relevant even as the hospitality industry evolves. "The rise of AI makes authentic human connection and memorable guest experiences more important than ever,” Gilson says. “By blending our signature human-centered philosophy with top-tier business education, Paul College is preparing leaders whose impact will extend far beyond traditional hospitality.” For Boulanger, it comes down to something simple. “People will always value human connection,” Boulanger says. “A warm welcome, a thoughtful gesture, or someone taking the time to make you feel special can turn an ordinary visit into a lasting memory.” Current Role and Employer: Sales & Catering Coordinator @ Omni Parker HousePrevious Roles: Pool Bar/Restaurant Supervisor @ Wentworth by the Sea Resort; Catering Wait Staff @ Phillips Exeter AcademyUNH Activities and Student Organizations: President of Eta Sigma Delta – International Hospitality & Tourism Management Honor Society; Dean’s Ambassador – Peter T. Paul College of Business and Economics; Peer Advisor & Teaching Assistant – University Advising Center; CHAARG Member What experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on you?Although many experiences and opportunities in UNH’s hospitality management program have impacted me, being president of Eta Sigma Delta truly helped me get to where I am today. The honor society gave me confidence that I can be a true leader and guide others. My proudest moment was leading our hotel crawl down in Boston in December 2025. Little did I know I would be working at one of the hotels we toured that day (Omni Parker House). What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?I think artificial Intelligence (AI) will impact the hospitality industry in the future. With its rapid advancements, AI can do pretty much anything when it comes to looking up information, writing short summaries, or giving advice like a normal friend would. Although AI can assist with many everyday tasks of hospitality associates, the great thing about this industry is that the hospitality world revolves around real, live people. Something that AI can’t replace! What sets the hospitality industry apart is that human interaction makes a guest’s stay special. Without it, I believe that hotels would never be the same. I can see AI shaping the industry’s future, but I don’t see it replacing it. Current Role and Employer: Group Sales Manager @ Raffles BostonPrevious Roles: Accounting Intern @ Chatham Bars Inn; Sales & Marketing Coordinator @ Raffles Boston (pre-opening and opening team).UNH Activities and Student Organizations: Eta Sigma Delta; Kappa Delta What experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on you?One of the most valuable aspects of UNH's hospitality management program was the opportunity to connect with industry professionals through guest speaker presentations. Those connections truly helped shape my career and ultimately led me to where I am today. I learned early on the importance of asking thoughtful questions, connecting with guest speakers on LinkedIn, and maintaining those relationships beyond the classroom. A connection I made with a guest speaker led to an internship opportunity at Chatham Bars Inn, which ultimately opened the door for me to join the pre-opening team at Raffles Boston, the first Raffles property in North and South America. Being part of opening such an iconic property right out of college was an incredible opportunity and one that has played a significant role in my career. What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?As technology and AI continue to become a bigger part of our everyday lives, I think we’ll see an even greater emphasis on building genuine, in-person relationships within the hospitality industry. While technology brings so many exciting opportunities to make our jobs easier and more efficient, I believe the personal connections we make will become more valuable than ever. Especially in luxury hospitality, it's often the smallest, most thoughtful gestures and genuine interactions that leave the biggest impression. At the end of the day, hospitality is all about people, and I think that’s something technology will never replace. Current Role and Employer: General Manager @ Wentworth by the Sea Opal Collection ResortPrevious Roles: Hotel Manager @ Omni Parker House; Director of Rooms @ Omni Boston Hotel at the Seaport; Assistant General Manager @ Kimpton Nine Zero HotelUNH Activities and Student Organizations: UNH Board of Young Hospitality Professionals; UNH International Hospitality Advisory Board; UNH Hospitality Management Mentor ProgramWhat experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on your career?My operations internship at the Omni Parker House through UNH was a launching point for my career, solidifying my passion for hotel operations and introducing me to mentor and fellow UNH alumnus John Murtha. That experience led to my acceptance into Omni’s Leader in Development program, and just two days after graduation, I began my career at the Omni Berkshire Place in New York City. Another influential mentor was Professor Carl Lindblade, who led the internship program and helped open that first door. His continued guidance has remained invaluable, specifically throughout my work with historic properties, including both the Omni Parker House and Wentworth by the Sea. As a full-circle connection, I recently learned Carl was once an intern at the Wentworth himself. What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?I believe one of the biggest shifts in hospitality is the growing focus on more personalized guest experiences. Today's technology helps us better understand guest preferences, anticipate needs, and tailor stays in meaningful ways. Whether it's recognizing a returning guest or recommending experiences that match their interests, these insights allow us to deliver a higher level of service. The technology provides the information, but it's our associates who turn it into genuine hospitality and memorable experiences. Current Role and Employer: General Manager of Graduate by Hilton Providence @ HighgatePrevious Roles: General Manager @ Highgate; Director of Sales @ Highgate; Housekeeping and Front Desk Roles @ Kimpton Hotels UNH Activities and Student Organizations: Greek Affairs Chair on Student Senate What experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on your career?My internship with Starwood Hotels was pivotal in my hotel journey. What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?Of course it’s AI, but so many hospitality companies are already using it the wrong way. The future of hospitality will depend partly on whether we use AI to create more human connection or remove it. As hotel roles become more consolidated, anyone not using AI to jumpstart everyday tasks will fall behind. The opportunity is to use it smartly to save time and energy, without replacing the personal connections that hospitality is built on. Current Role and Employer: Group Sales Manager @ Virgin Hotels Dallas in Dallas, Texas.Previous Roles: Corporate Catering Sales Manager @ Hotel Crescent Court, also located in Dallas. (One of my career highlights during my time there was securing my first $100,000 contract for a production associated with the television series Landman, which filmed a scene at the property)UNH Activities and Student Organizations: Alpha Phi Omega (APO), Hospitality Financial and Technology Professionals (HFTP) What experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on your career?Without a doubt, Gourmet Dinner! It was such a unique opportunity to experience firsthand the amount of planning, collaboration, and attention to detail that goes into executing a successful hospitality event. Being able to take what we learned in the classroom and apply it to a real event was invaluable. Looking back on my career, especially now that I work in hotel sales and regularly coordinate with multiple departments to bring group programs and events to life, I can appreciate just how much that experience prepared me for the realities of the hospitality industry. What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?I am particularly fascinated by the growing role of artificial intelligence in hospitality and its potential to revolutionize how hotels operate. From streamlining reporting and administrative tasks to improving forecasting and helping teams analyze business opportunities, I believe AI has the potential to make hotel operations significantly more efficient. Hospitality will always be a people-focused industry, and I think one of the most exciting opportunities is finding ways to use technology to support our teams behind the scenes, allowing us to dedicate more time and attention to creating exceptional guest experiences. Current Role and Employer: Regional Director of Operations @ LEVY Previous Roles: Vice President Hospitality Strategy @ LEVY at Mercedes-Benz Stadium (Atlanta, GA); Director of Operations @ LEVY at Kaseya Center (Miami, FL). Prior to my Sports and Entertainment career, I was with Ocean Properties Hotels & Resorts for eight years at several flagship locations.UNH Activities and Student Organizations: Eta Sigma Delta Honor Society What experience or opportunity through UNH's hospitality management program had the greatest impact on you?One of the experiences that stands out most from my time at UNH was the Gourmet Dinner class, where students were responsible for planning and executing a high-end catered event, taking on various front- and back-of-house roles. It was a tremendous opportunity to experience firsthand the importance of teamwork, communication, and attention to detail in delivering exceptional hospitality. More importantly, it reinforced something that has stayed with me throughout my career: hospitality is ultimately a people business. Building meaningful relationships with your teams, guests, and business partners is just as important as operational execution. That foundation has carried with me from hotels and resorts to leading operations across some of the country's largest sports and entertainment venues. What changes or opportunities do you see shaping the future of the hospitality industry?I believe the future of hospitality will be defined by our ability to create more personalized, memorable experiences while continuing to evolve how we operate. Technology, data, and changing consumer expectations will undoubtedly reshape our industry, particularly in sports and entertainment, where guests increasingly expect experiences that go well beyond the event itself. However, as the industry becomes more sophisticated, the human element of hospitality will only become more important. Our greatest opportunity as leaders is to embrace innovation while investing in our people, developing future leaders, and building cultures where genuine hospitality can thrive. Ultimately, the organizations that find the right balance between innovation, operational excellence, and meaningful human connections will be the ones that set themselves apart. The quarterly results were aided by the strength witnessed in Optum Insight and Optum Rx. Medical cost management, pricing discipline and benefit design changes also contributed to the upside. However, weakness in Optum Health and declining memberships partially offset the positives. UnitedHealth's third-quarter premium of $87.1 billion decreased from $89 billion a year ago but beat the consensus mark of $86 billion. UNH's adjusted medical care ratio (MCR) was 88.4% in the third quarter, which improved 150 bps from the year-ago period. MCR witnessed a decrease, backed by solid medical cost management, pricing discipline and benefit design changes. Medical costs of $77 billion declined from $80 billion a year ago. Third-quarter total operating costs of $106.1 billion decreased 2.5% year over year, benefiting from lower medical costs and operating costs. However, the figure was higher than our model estimate of $104.5 billion. The third-quarter 2026 operating cost ratio improved to 12.8% from 13.5% a year ago. UnitedHealth's adjusted operating earnings rose 45.2% year over year to $6.3 billion in the third quarter. Revenues of the health benefits business of UnitedHealth, UnitedHealthcare, declined 0.8% year over year to $86.3 billion in the third quarter. However, the metric beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $84.7 billion and our estimate of $82.8 billion. The UnitedHealthcare business catered to 48.3 million people as of Sept. 30, 2026, which fell 3.6% year over year. Adjusted earnings from operations amounted to $2.7 billion, up from $1.8 billion a year ago. The adjusted operating margin increased to 3.1% from 2.1% a year ago. Revenues in the Optum business line were $66.9 billion, which fell from $69.2 billion a year ago due to lower contribution from Optum Health. The figure missed the consensus mark of $67.1 billion. Optum's adjusted earnings from operations rose to $3.6 billion from $2.5 billion a year ago. The adjusted operating margin of 5.3% increased from 3.6%. UnitedHealth exited the third quarter with cash and short-term investments of $28.5 billion, which rose from the 2025-end level of $28.1 billion. Total assets of $312.8 billion increased from the $309.6 billion figure at 2025-end. Long-term debt, less current maturities, amounted to $68.7 billion, down from the $72.3 billion figure as of Dec. 31, 2025. Short-term borrowings and the current maturities of long-term debt were $5.6 billion. Total equity of $104.1 billion advanced from the 2025-end level of $100.1 billion. UnitedHealth generated operating cash flows of $25.1 billion in the first nine months of 2026, which grew from the prior-year figure of $18.6 billion. In the first nine months of 2026, it paid dividends worth $6.2 billion and repurchased $5 billion of stock. Management earlier anticipated revenues for 2026 above $439 billion, which are below the 2025 level due to planned right-sizing across operations. Adjusted EPS is now expected to be at least $20.5 for 2026, up from the previously guided range of $19.5-$20, indicating improving margins. Net margin was expected to be around 3.6%, up from 2.7% in 2025. The company earlier expected MCR to be 88.1% (± 25 bps) in 2026, down from 89.1% in 2025. The operating cost ratio was likely to be 12.8% (± 50 bps) in 2026. The tax rate was expected to be around 18.5%. Operating cash flows were estimated to be around $24 billion, up from the previous guidance of greater than $18 billion. UNH was expected to make repurchases of at least $5 billion and pay dividends worth $8 billion in 2026. Capital expenditure was estimated at $3.8 billion for the year. Furthermore, management earlier expected medical memberships to be within 46.945-47.495 million in 2026, with significant declines in commercial risk, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid heads.
